imageInfo.caption: Eric IV Ploughpenny enthroned with a saint’s halo, in a wall painting of about 1300 in Saint Bendt’s Church, Ringsted, where he was buried and venerated as a saint.
imageInfo.creator: Unknown Danish wall painter
imageInfo.note: Wall painting (kalkmaleri) in Sankt Bendts Kirke, Ringsted, from the cult of Saint Eric that grew up at his tomb; the church’s monumental paintings over his grave are dated to about 1300. Painted about fifty years after his murder in 1250, as a devotional image rather than a likeness. The Commons photograph is licensed GPL.

overview: Eric IV of Denmark was Danish king remembered for internal conflict and the tax nickname Ploughpenny. The profile is anchored by concrete turning points: 1241 — Becomes king; 1240s — Conflict with nobles and brothers; 1250 — Murdered.
He died in 1250, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Overview

He died in 1250, and his reign belongs to the wider story of Scandinavian state formation, Christianization, dynastic conflict, and northern Europe’s ties to England, the Baltic, and the Empire.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Eric IV of Denmark was born c. 1216. His family background is usually placed in House of Estridsen, though early Scandinavian genealogy can be uncertain and politically shaped.

Eric IV of Denmark's early life belonged to the medieval Scandinavian world, where kinship, sea routes, church contacts, assemblies, and armed followings shaped the opportunities available to a ruler.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Eric IV of Denmark, nicknamed Ploughpenny after a hated tax he is said to have imposed, is remembered through the bitter dynastic strife of his reign and a violent death. The sources present a king locked in relentless war with his own brothers over the division of the realm, and the tax-nickname suggests a ruler resented for fiscal demands.

His reign ended in murder: he was killed, by tradition at the hands of agents of his brother Abel, his body reportedly thrown into a fjord. The fratricidal context — Abel swore an oath denying involvement that few believed — gave the episode a dark notoriety in Danish memory.

Little survives of Eric's personality beyond the resentment captured in his nickname and the impression of a king consumed by family conflict. He is remembered less as an individual than as a figure in a violent dynastic tragedy, the victim of a brother's ambition, and the unpopular tax fixed to his name is most of the personal trace that endures.

contentSections.title: As king of Denmark
paragraphs: Eric IV ruled during a period of noble and dynastic conflict. His taxation and disputes with his brothers made his reign unstable.
As King of Denmark, Eric IV of Denmark had to turn dynastic claim into workable authority through alliances, military pressure, church support, and acceptance by regional elites.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Murdered in 1250, traditionally after capture near the Schlei by supporters of his brother Abel; the killing intensified Danish dynastic conflict.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: His violent death deepened Danish dynastic conflict and became part of royal martyr-like memory.
Later saga, saintly, or national traditions often amplified Eric IV of Denmark's reputation, so the article separates near-contemporary evidence from later memory where possible.

timeline.title: Born
timeline.description: Eric IV of Denmark was born around c. 1216, but the birthplace is not securely recorded. The date is approximate, but it places the early life in the setting of Kingdom of Denmark.

timeline.title: Becomes king
timeline.description: Eric IV became king after Valdemar II, inheriting a kingdom where royal taxation and aristocratic resistance were increasingly explosive.

timeline.title: Conflict with nobles and brothers
timeline.description: Eric’s reign was marked by taxation disputes and dynastic conflict, especially with powerful brothers and aristocratic opponents.

timeline.title: Murdered
timeline.description: Eric was killed in 1250 after conflict with his brother Abel, turning royal family rivalry into a succession crisis.

timeline.title: Dies
timeline.description: Eric was murdered in 1250, traditionally after capture by his brother Abel’s supporters.
